1a.question: With a = [16, 16] and b = [176, 16] (subpixels), what is edge(a, b, p) for the centre of pixel (5, 0)?
1a.format: a whole number, such as 512 or -512
1a.reason: The centre of pixel (5, 0) is (5.5, 0.5), so p = [88, 8] in subpixels. edge(a, b, p) = (176 - 16)(8 - 16) - (16 - 16)(88 - 16) = 160 × (-8) - 0 = -1,280. It is negative because walking from a to b runs right along y = 1, and the centre at y 0.5 lies on the right of that walk.

wrong.feedback: The size is right and the sign is not. Walking from a to b goes right, and the centre at y 0.5 is below the line y = 1, which is on your right: the edge function is negative there.
That is the value in pixel units. The edge function works on subpixels, 16 to a pixel, so every coordinate is 16 times larger and the product 256 times larger.
That uses the pixel's corner [80, 0]. A pixel is tested at its centre, (5.5, 0.5), which is [88, 8] in subpixels.
The centre isn't on the line: the line runs along y = 1, and the centre of pixel (5, 0) is at y 0.5.

1a2.question: A fresh case. With a = [32, 0] and b = [32, 160] (subpixels), what is edge(a, b, p) for the centre of pixel (3, 1)?
1a2.format: a whole number, such as 512 or -512
1a2.reason: The centre of pixel (3, 1) is [56, 24]. edge(a, b, p) = (32 - 32)(24 - 0) - (160 - 0)(56 - 32) = 0 - 160 × 24 = -3,840. Walking up along x = 2, the centre at x 3.5 is on your right, so the value is negative.

wrong.feedback: Walking from a to b goes up, and the centre at x 3.5 lies to the right of x = 2: right of the walk means negative.
That mixes units: one factor is in subpixels and the other in pixels, as in 160 × 1.5. Put every coordinate in subpixels, 16 to a pixel.

1b.question: A triangle's corners have x at 3.5, 20.625 and 12.5 pixels. How many columns does its bounding box visit?
1b.reason: In subpixels the corners are at x 56, 330 and 200. The box starts at floor(56 / 16) = 3 and stops before ceil(330 / 16) = 21, so it visits columns 3 to 20: 18 columns. Column 20 is needed because its centre, 20.5, is left of the corner at 20.625.

wrong.feedback: That stops before floor(330 / 16) = 20 and loses column 20. Its centre, 20.5, is left of the corner at 20.625, so a centre there can be inside: the end is rounded up.
The end, ceil(330 / 16) = 21, is excluded: the box visits columns 3 to 20, which is 18.
The box holds whole columns: from floor(56 / 16) = 3 up to, not including, ceil(330 / 16) = 21.

1b2.question: A fresh case. A triangle's corners have x at 0.25, 9.5 and 5 pixels. How many columns does its bounding box visit?
1b2.reason: In subpixels the corners are at x 4, 152 and 80. The box runs from floor(4 / 16) = 0 up to, not including, ceil(152 / 16) = 10: columns 0 to 9, which is 10. Column 9's centre, 9.5, sits exactly on the corner's x, so it has to be tested.

wrong.feedback: That stops at floor(152 / 16) = 9 and loses column 9, whose centre at 9.5 can still be covered (it is exactly the corner's x).
The end, ceil(152 / 16) = 10, is excluded: columns 0 to 9.

1c.question: The square with corners (8.5, 7.5) and (56.5, 55.5) is cut along its diagonal from (8.5, 55.5) to (56.5, 7.5) into two triangles. If every edge counted a centre on it as inside (w >= 0 on every edge), how many pixels would both triangles draw?
1c.reason: The diagonal from (8.5, 55.5) to (56.5, 7.5) passes through the centres (8.5, 55.5), (9.5, 54.5) and so on down to (56.5, 7.5): 56 - 8 + 1 = 49 centres, both end corners included. Each lies on the shared edge, so with >= both triangles draw it. Centres on the outer edges belong to one triangle only, so they are drawn once.

wrong.feedback: Count both ends: the centres run from (8.5, 55.5) to (56.5, 7.5), one column at a time, which is 56 - 8 + 1 = 49.
The two end corners are corners of both triangles, and with >= on every edge both triangles include them too: 49 in all.
That counts each drawing. The question asks for pixels: 49 pixels, each drawn by both triangles.
With > on every edge no pixel would be drawn twice, but the diagonal's centres would be lost. With >=, both triangles draw each of them.

1c2.question: A fresh case. A square with corners (4.5, 10.5) and (40.5, 46.5) is cut along the diagonal between those corners. With >= on every edge, how many pixels do both triangles draw?
1c2.reason: The diagonal steps one pixel right and one up from (4.5, 10.5) to (40.5, 46.5), passing through 40 - 4 + 1 = 37 centres, each drawn by both triangles.

wrong.feedback: Count both ends: 40 - 4 + 1 = 37.
That counts drawings. 37 pixels are each drawn twice.

1d.question: Each of these is an edge a -> b of a counter-clockwise triangle. Which own their ties? (a) a -> b runs straight down, (b) straight up, (c) straight right, (d) straight left.
1d.format: the letters of the edges that own their ties, such as a,b, or none
1d.reason: The interior is on the left of a -> b. Going down (a), the left is +x, so the nudge right moves inside: it owns. Going up (b), the interior is to the left (-x): no. Going right (c), the interior is above, and the e * e part of the nudge moves up into it: it owns. Going left (d), the interior is below: no. In owns, (a) has gx > 0, (b) gx < 0, (c) gx = 0 and gy > 0, (d) gx = 0 and gy < 0.

wrong.feedback: That is the mirrored rule, the nudge left and down. The course's rule nudges right and up: an edge going down has its interior on the right, and an edge going right has it above.
Edge (d), going left, has its interior below it, and the nudge moves up, out of the triangle. Edge (c), going right, has its interior above, so it owns its ties.
Edge (b), going up, has its interior on the left (-x), and the nudge moves right, out. Edge (a), going down, has its interior on the right: it owns.
Edge (c) owns too: a horizontal edge going right has the interior above it, and the e * e part of the nudge moves up into it.
Edge (a) owns too: going straight down, the interior lies to the right (+x), where the nudge moves.
Every tie must go to exactly one triangle, so the edges that own are the ones whose interior the nudge (right, and a tinier bit up) moves into: (a) and (c).

1d2.question: A fresh case. Edges a -> b of counter-clockwise triangles: (a) runs down and to the right at 45°, (b) up and to the left, (c) up and to the right, (d) down and to the left. Which own their ties?
1d2.format: the letters of the edges that own their ties, such as a,b, or none
1d2.reason: gx = -(b.y - a.y) is positive whenever the edge goes down, whatever its x direction: (a) and (d). Their interiors lie on the +x side of the edge, where the nudge moves. Edges going up, (b) and (c), have gx < 0.

wrong.feedback: Those go up, so gx = -(b.y - a.y) is negative: the interior is on the -x side and the nudge moves away from it.
Edge (c) goes up, so gx < 0. Only the vertical part decides here. gy matters only when gx is 0.

1e.question: A corner sits at x 5.28 pixels. Where does snap2 put it, in pixels?
1e.format: a number of pixels, such as 3.75
1e.reason: snap2 rounds x × 16 to the nearest integer: 5.28 × 16 = 84.48, which rounds to 84, and 84 / 16 = 5.25. Every corner lands on a multiple of 1/16 pixel before any edge value is computed, the same grid the GPU snaps to.

wrong.feedback: snap2 rounds to the nearest 1/16 pixel before any edge value is computed: 5.28 × 16 = 84.48, which rounds to 84, or 5.25 pixels.
That rounds 84.48 up to 85. snap2 rounds to the nearest: 84, which is 5.25 pixels.
The grid is 1/16 pixel, not a whole pixel: 5.28 × 16 = 84.48 rounds to 84, which is 5.25.
The grid is 1/16 pixel, not a pixel centre: 5.28 × 16 = 84.48 rounds to 84, which is 5.25.

1e2.question: A fresh case. A corner sits at x 12.97 pixels. Where does snap2 put it, in pixels?

wrong.feedback: That rounds 207.52 down to 207. Math.round gives 208, which is 13 pixels.
That is the subpixel integer. In pixels it is 208 / 16 = 13.

1t.section: A vertex shared by six triangles
1t.question: Six triangles meet at the centre of pixel (32, 32), at (32.5, 32.5). Their outer corners in counter-clockwise order are r0 (52.5, 32.5), r1 (42.5, 50.5), r2 (22.5, 50.5), r3 (12.5, 32.5), r4 (22.5, 14.5) and r5 (42.5, 14.5). Triangle k has the centre, rk and the next outer corner in that order as its corners. Which triangle owns pixel (32, 32)?
1t.reason: The centre lies on two edges of every one of the six triangles. Nudged right by e and up by e * e, it moves just above the line from the centre to r0, which points straight right. Triangle 0 lies between r0 and r1, above that line, so it owns the pixel. Triangle 5, between r5 and r0, lies below it.

wrong.feedback: Triangle 5 lies below the line from the centre to r0. The nudge moves right and a tinier amount up, so it lands in triangle 0, just above that line.
The nudge moves right, towards r0, not left towards r3.
The nudge moves right, towards r0. Triangle 2 lies on the left.
Triangle 1 lies between r1 and r2, up and to the left. The nudge goes right and only a tiny bit up, so it lands between r0 and r1: triangle 0.
Every centre inside a fan belongs to exactly one of its triangles, and the nudge picks which.

1t2.question: A fresh case. Four triangles meet at the centre of pixel (10, 10). Their outer corners, counter-clockwise, are r0 (10.5, 20.5) straight up, r1 (0.5, 10.5) left, r2 (10.5, 0.5) down and r3 (20.5, 10.5) right. Triangle k has the centre, rk and the next corner round. Which triangle owns pixel (10, 10)?
1t2.reason: The nudge moves the centre right and a tinier amount up, just above the line towards r3. Triangle 3 lies between r3 (right) and r0 (up), so it owns the pixel.

wrong.feedback: Triangle 2 lies between down and right, below the line towards r3. The nudge moves up a little, into triangle 3.
Triangle 0 lies between up and left. The nudge moves right.

2a.question: With the camera of examples/clip-trace.mjs (perspective(60, 160 / 120, 0.1, 100), the eye at the origin, a 160 by 120 picture), a point sits 10 m ahead and 2 m to the left, at (-2, 0, -10). Which pixel column does it land in?
2a.reason: Clip x is -2 × 1.299 = -2.598 and w is 10, so x / w = -0.260: the mirror of the traced point, which had x / w = 0.260 (twice as far to the side, twice as far away). The window x is (1 - 0.260) / 2 × 160 = 59.19 pixels, in column 59.

wrong.feedback: That is the traced point's column. This point is to the left, so x / w is -0.260 and it lands at 160 - 100.81 = 59.19.
It isn't at the centre: twice as far to the side and twice as far away gives the same size of x / w as the traced point, 0.260, on the left.
The window x is 59.19 pixels, which is in column 59: a column holds x from 59 up to 60.
x / w is -2.598 / 10 = -0.260, not -0.5: perspective scales x by 1.299, and the point is 10 m away.

2a2.question: A fresh case. Same camera. A point sits 20 m ahead and 2 m to the right, at (2, 0, -20). Which pixel column does it land in?
2a2.reason: Clip x is 2 × 1.299 = 2.598 and w is 20, so x / w = 0.130, half the traced point's. The window x is (1 + 0.130) / 2 × 160 = 90.4 pixels, in column 90.

wrong.feedback: This point is four times as far away as the traced one but only twice as far to the side, so x / w is half as big: 0.130.
The window x is 90.4 pixels: column 90.

2b.question: A clip point is (0.5, -0.25, 0, 1) and the picture is 160 by 120. What x does toWindow return, in subpixels?
2b.reason: x / w = 0.5, which maps to (0.5 + 1) / 2 × 160 = 120 pixels. In subpixels that is 120 × 16 = 1,920, already a whole number, so rounding leaves it.

wrong.feedback: That is in pixels. toWindow returns subpixels: 120 × 16 = 1,920.
x / w = 0.5 maps to (0.5 + 1) / 2 of the width, not 0.5 / 2: the range -1..1 is moved to 0..2 first.
That uses the height. x is mapped with the width, 160: (0.5 + 1) / 2 × 160 × 16 = 1,920.
That is y: (-0.25 + 1) / 2 × 120 × 16. The question asks for x.

2b2.question: A fresh case. A clip point is (-0.5, 0.5, 0, 2) and the picture is 160 by 120. What x does toWindow return, in subpixels?
2b2.reason: Divide by w first: x / w = -0.25, which maps to (-0.25 + 1) / 2 × 160 = 60 pixels, 960 subpixels.

wrong.feedback: Divide by w before mapping: -0.5 / 2 = -0.25, not -0.5.
That is in pixels: 60 × 16 = 960 subpixels.

2c.question: With the trace's camera, take the point 2 m behind the eye and 1 m to the right, (1, 0, 2). Where does the divide put it? (a) off the screen, (b) in the right half, (c) in the left half, (d) at the centre.
2c.reason: Its clip w is -2, the negative of its distance behind the eye. Clip x is 1.299, so x / w = -0.650: the sign flips and the point lands left of centre, at about 28 pixels, inside the picture. A triangle with a corner behind the eye is therefore drawn mirrored across the screen unless it is clipped first.

wrong.feedback: x / w is -0.650, between -1 and 1, so the divide puts it inside the picture: w is -2 and flips the sign.
The point is to the right, but its w is negative (-2), so x / w = 1.299 / -2 = -0.650, left of centre.
x / w is -0.650, not 0: the point is 1 m to the side, and the negative w flips it to the left.

2c2.question: A fresh case. The point is 3 m behind the eye and 1 m to the left, (-1, 0, 3). Where does the divide put it? (a) off the screen, (b) right half, (c) left half, (d) centre.
2c2.reason: w = -3 and clip x = -1.299, so x / w = 0.433: a point behind you on the left lands in the right half.

wrong.feedback: The point is to the left, but w = -3 is negative, so x / w = -1.299 / -3 = 0.433, right of centre.

2d.question: A triangle's corners have z + w of 0.6, -0.2 and 0.6. On the edge v0 -> v1, at what fraction t of the way from v0 is the cut?
2d.format: a number between 0 and 1, such as 0.4
2d.reason: t = d_s / (d_s - d_e) = 0.6 / (0.6 - (-0.2)) = 0.6 / 0.8 = 0.75. Along the edge, z + w falls by 0.8 in all and reaches 0 once it has fallen 0.6, which is 0.6 / 0.8 = 0.75 of the way.

wrong.feedback: That is measured from v1. From v0, t = 0.6 / (0.6 + 0.2) = 0.75.
The cut isn't halfway: v0 is three times as far in front (0.6) as v1 is behind (0.2), so the cut is three quarters of the way.

2d2.question: A fresh case. Corners have z + w of 0.3, 0.9 and -0.6. On the edge v1 -> v2, at what fraction t of the way from v1 is the cut?

wrong.feedback: That is measured from v2. From v1, t = 0.9 / 1.5 = 0.6.
1.5 is d_s - d_e, the bottom of the fraction on its own. Divide d_s by it: t = 0.9 / 1.5.

2e.question: A clipped piece of the floor has an edge a -> b from (40, 8) to (8, 40) in pixels, and its interior is on the left of that direction. Does the edge own its ties? Answer yes or no.
2e.reason: The edge goes up and to the left, so gx = -(b.y - a.y) = -(40 - 8) = -32 is negative: the interior lies on the -x side, and the nudge right moves away from it. The tie rule from lesson 1 works the same on clipped and snapped corners.

wrong.feedback: gx = -(40 - 8) = -32 is negative. The edge goes up, its interior is on the left, and the nudge moves right, out of the triangle.

2e2.question: A fresh case. An edge a -> b runs from (8, 40) to (40, 8) in pixels, with the interior on its left. Does it own its ties?
2e2.reason: Going down and to the right, gx = -(8 - 40) = 32 is positive: the interior lies to the right, where the nudge moves.

wrong.feedback: gx = -(b.y - a.y) = -(8 - 40) = 32, positive: an edge going down has its interior on the +x side.

2f.question: A corner lies exactly on the far plane, where clip z equals w. What depth z does toWindow give it?
2f.reason: On the far plane z / w = 1, and toWindow maps it to (1 + 1) / 2 = 1, the largest depth, the value the depth buffer is cleared to in lesson 3. A corner on the near plane gets (-1 + 1) / 2 = 0.

wrong.feedback: 0 is the near plane, where z = -w. On the far plane z / w = 1, so the depth is (1 + 1) / 2 = 1.
toWindow's z is z / w mapped to 0..1, not metres: (1 + 1) / 2 = 1.
0.5 is z / w = 0, which is not on either plane. On the far plane z / w = 1.

2f2.question: A fresh case. A corner lies exactly on the near plane, where clip z equals -w. What depth z does toWindow give it, up to rounding?
2f2.reason: z / w = -1 on the near plane, and (-1 + 1) / 2 = 0.

wrong.feedback: 1 is the far plane. On the near plane z / w = -1, so the depth is 0.
toWindow maps z / w = -1 to (-1 + 1) / 2 = 0.

3a.question: A triangle has a red corner v0, a green corner v1 and a blue corner v2, with w = 1 at all three. At one pixel the edge values are 20, 30 and 50. What level does the pixel's green channel get?
3a.reason: The weights are 20 / 100, 30 / 100 and 50 / 100. Green comes only from v1, so green = 0.3, and toByte gives Math.round(0.3 × 255) = Math.round(76.5) = 77.

wrong.feedback: 0.3 × 255 = 76.5, and toByte rounds to the nearest level, with .5 going up: 77.
The weight is 0.3, and the stored level is 0.3 × 255 rounded, 77.
The green channel takes v1's weight only, 0.3, not an average of the three.
Green comes from v1 alone, weighted 30 / 100 = 0.3, so the level is 0.3 × 255 rounded, 77.

3a2.question: A fresh case. Same corners, w = 1 at all three, edge values 70, 20 and 10. What level does the blue channel get?
3a2.reason: Blue comes from v2, whose weight is 10 / 100 = 0.1. 0.1 × 255 = 25.5, which rounds to 26.

wrong.feedback: 25.5 rounds to the nearest level, with .5 going up: 26.
That is v1's weight, 0.2. Blue comes from v2, weight 0.1.

3b.question: Lesson 1's `one-triangle` scene, coloured red, green and blue at its corners, with clip w of 1, 6 and 2.5. Blend its colour by screen weights alone and compare with the correct picture. What is the largest difference in any channel? (a) 0 or 1 level, (b) about 10, (c) about 50, (d) over 100.
3b.reason: The green corner is six times as far away as the red one, so the divide by w squeezes the far part of the surface into few pixels, and screen weights spread the far corner's colour over too many of them: the largest difference is 107 of 255 levels, at pixel (43, 47), and every one of the 1,330 pixels differs by more than a level.

wrong.feedback: With all three w equal the two blends would agree. Here w runs from 1 to 6, and the difference reaches 107 levels.
The far corner is six times as far away as the near one, and screen weights alone put colours off by up to 107 levels.
It is larger: 107 levels at the worst pixel, with every pixel off by more than 1.

3b2.question: A fresh case. The same triangle with clip w = 4 at all three corners. What is the largest difference between screen-weight blending and perspective-correct blending? (a) 0 or 1 level, (b) about 10, (c) about 50, (d) over 100.
3b2.reason: With equal w, each q_i is b_i / 4, and dividing by their sum cancels the 4: the perspective-correct blend equals the screen blend. Only rounding can differ.

wrong.feedback: The error comes from w differing between corners. With w = 4 at all three, the 1/w factors cancel.

3c.question: An edge runs from a corner with w = 1 and texture coordinate u = 0 to a corner with w = 3 and u = 1. What u does the pixel halfway between them on screen get?
3c.reason: The screen weights are 0.5 and 0.5, so q = 0.5 × 1 and 0.5 × 1/3 = 0.167. u = (0.5 × 0 + 0.167 × 1) / (0.5 + 0.167) = 0.167 / 0.667 = 0.25. Halfway on screen is a quarter of the way along the edge in 3D.

wrong.feedback: That is the screen-weight blend. Weight each corner by 1 / w first: q = 0.5 and 0.167, so u = 0.167 / 0.667 = 0.25.
That gives the near corner the smaller weight. The far corner, w = 3, gets it: 0.5 / 3, so u = 0.25.
Divide by the sum of the q weights, 0.667: u = 0.167 / 0.667 = 0.25.

3c2.question: A fresh case. From w = 1, u = 0 to w = 4, u = 1. What u does the pixel halfway on screen get?

wrong.feedback: Weight each corner by 1 / w: q = 0.5 and 0.125, so u = 0.125 / 0.625 = 0.2.
Divide by the sum 0.625: 0.2.

3d.section: Equal depth keeps the first draw
3d.question: A red triangle is drawn, then a green copy at exactly the same depths. Suppose the test used <= instead of <, the rule WebGL calls LEQUAL. How many of the red copy's 1,492 pixels would the green copy win? (a) none, (b) about half, (c) all of them.
3d.reason: Every pixel of the copy has exactly the stored depth, and <= lets an equal depth pass, so green wins all 1,492. Under LESS it wins none, which is what both measured GPUs do.

wrong.feedback: That is LESS. With <=, an equal depth passes, and every pixel of the copy is equal.

The depths are equal at every pixel, not just some, so the rule decides all 1,492 the same way. About half, 771 of the 1,492 in the check's pair, is what comparing unrounded float64 depths against the stored float32 depths gives.

3d2.question: A fresh case. Under LESS, the green copy is drawn first and the red one second, at the same depths. Which colour shows? (a) red, (b) green, (c) half each.
3d2.reason: Under LESS the second draw loses every tie, so whichever copy came first stays: green.

wrong.feedback: Under LESS an equal depth fails the test, so the second draw, red, loses every pixel.

3e.question: A corner's clip coordinates have z = 2 and w = 4. What depth does toWindow give it?
3e.reason: toWindow divides first, z / w = 0.5, then maps -1..1 to 0..1: (0.5 + 1) / 2 = 0.75.

wrong.feedback: That is z / w. toWindow then maps it from -1..1 to 0..1: (0.5 + 1) / 2 = 0.75.
That is 1 / w, which toWindow keeps as invW. The depth is (z / w + 1) / 2 = 0.75.
Divide by 2 after adding 1: (0.5 + 1) / 2 = 0.75.

3e2.question: A fresh case. Clip z = -3 and w = 5. What depth does toWindow give?

wrong.feedback: That is z / w. Mapped to 0..1 it is (-0.6 + 1) / 2 = 0.2.

3f.question: Which expression gives d, the distance in front of the eye, at a pixel, where b0, b1 and b2 are the screen weights and w0, w1 and w2 the corners' clip w? (a) b0 w0 + b1 w1 + b2 w2, (b) 1 / (b0/w0 + b1/w1 + b2/w2), (c) b0 z0 + b1 z1 + b2 z2, using the window depths, (d) (w0 + w1 + w2) / 3.
3f.reason: d is an attribute that varies evenly across the surface in 3D, so it needs the perspective-correct blend: (b0 w0/w0 + b1 w1/w1 + b2 w2/w2) / (b0/w0 + b1/w1 + b2/w2). The top is b0 + b1 + b2 = 1, which leaves 1 / (b0/w0 + b1/w1 + b2/w2): the interpolated 1/w, turned over.

wrong.feedback: That blends w by screen weights alone, the mistake that bent the floor. w varies evenly in 3D, so it needs the 1/w correction, which simplifies to 1 / (b0/w0 + b1/w1 + b2/w2).
Window depth, (z / w + 1) / 2, runs from 0 to 1 and grows much faster near the eye than far away, so it isn't a distance in metres.
That is the same at every pixel of the triangle. d changes across it.

3f2.question: A fresh case. On the screen, a pixel lies halfway between a corner with w = 2 and a corner with w = 6 (weights 0.5 and 0.5, the third 0). What is d there?
3f2.reason: d = 1 / (0.5 / 2 + 0.5 / 6) = 1 / (0.25 + 0.083) = 3. Halfway on screen is only a quarter of the way from 2 m to 6 m.

wrong.feedback: That is w blended by screen weights. d = 1 / (0.5 / 2 + 0.5 / 6) = 3.
That is the interpolated 1/w. Turn it over: d = 3.

5a.question: In checker-branch.asm the if is instruction 7 (counting from 0). What number does assemble store in its match.else?
5a.format: a whole number, an instruction index
5a.reason: Counting from 0: the seven instructions before the if are 0 to 6, the if is 7, its three muls 8 to 10, and the else 11. Then come the three mads, 12 to 14, and the endif, 15, which goes in match.end. Comments, the .in line and blank lines make no instruction.

wrong.feedback: 15 is the endif, which goes in match.end. match.else is the else, instruction 11.
12 is the first mad, after the else. runLane jumps there when the if is false, but match.else holds the else itself: 11.
That counts text lines, or starts from 1. Targets are instruction numbers counted from 0: the else is 11.

5a2.question: A fresh case. Read scenes/shaders/escape.asm. Its loop is instruction 5 (counting from 0). What number does assemble store in its match.end?
5a2.format: a whole number, an instruction index
5a2.reason: Five instructions come before the loop (0 to 4), the loop is 5, its body runs from 6 to 17 (seven up to and including the break, then five more), and the endloop is 18.

wrong.feedback: 12 is the break. match.end is the endloop, instruction 18.
19 is the mul after the endloop. The endloop is 18.

5b.question: A register holds a = 1 + 2^-12. With two roundings, mad r1, r0, r0, -1 gives exactly 2^-11 = 0.00048828125. What does a fused version, with one rounding at the end, give? (a) the same 0.00048828125, (b) 0.00048834085, a little more, (c) 0, (d) a little less than 0.00048828125.
5b.reason: a × a = 1 + 2^-11 + 2^-24. A float32 near 1 has steps of 2^-23, so rounding the product alone drops the 2^-24, and subtracting 1 leaves 2^-11. 8d.reason: Immediate reads and writes depth and writes colour for every layer, about 24 bytes per pixel per layer, 5.75 layers deep: 2,887,008 bytes. Tiled writes colour once and pays binning: 195,312 bytes. 14.78 times.

wrong.feedback: Immediate pays for depth and colour on every one of about six layers, tiled for colour once and the bins: 14.78 times.
Six layers of depth reads, depth writes and colour writes add up to far more: 14.78 times.
Binning costs the tiled renderer 118,512 bytes, so it isn't free: 14.78 times, not 100.

8d2.question: A fresh case. About how many times the tiled renderer's bytes does the immediate renderer move on the courtyard at 160 by 120? (a) about the same, (b) about 3 times, (c) about 15 times, (d) about 100 times.
8d2.reason: The courtyard is shallower and its big floor triangles join many tiles: 576,704 bytes against 191,744, of which binning is 112,896. 3.01 times.

wrong.feedback: That is the overdraw scene, about six layers deep. The courtyard has less overdraw and more binning: 3.01 times.

8t.question: dustScene(1) is 20,000 triangles of about one pixel each. Once binning is counted, which renderer moves fewer bytes, with 16 by 16 tiles and with 64 by 64 tiles? (a) tiled at both sizes, (b) tiled at 64 by 64 only, (c) immediate at both sizes, (d) immediate at 64 by 64 only.
8t.reason: A one-pixel triangle costs the immediate renderer at most 96 bytes. Tiled, it costs a 64-byte record and 72 bytes per bin, at least 136. Immediate moves 1,655,936 bytes, tiled 3,049,016 with 16-pixel tiles and 2,842,016 with 64-pixel tiles.

wrong.feedback: Tiling saves on overdraw. Here there is little, and every triangle pays at least 136 bytes of binning: immediate wins at both sizes.
Bigger tiles help a little, since fewer triangles straddle an edge, but binning still costs more than immediate's 96 bytes a triangle.
Immediate wins at 16 by 16 too, by more: 3,049,016 tiled bytes against 1,655,936.

8t2.question: A fresh case. A one-pixel triangle binned to exactly one tile: how many bytes of binning traffic does it cost, record and entry, written and read?
8t2.reason: 64 bytes for its record written, 4 for its entry written, then 4 + 64 read back for that one entry: 136.

wrong.feedback: Binning writes the record and the entry, then reads both back for each entry: 68 + 68 = 136.
Add the 64-byte record written once: 136.

8e.section: A triangle bigger than a tile
8e.question: A triangle's corners have z + w of 0.5, -1.5 and 0.5. On the edge v0 -> v1, at what fraction t of the way from v0 does clipNear cut it?
8e.format: a number between 0 and 1, such as 0.4
8e.reason: t = d_s / (d_s - d_e) = 0.5 / (0.5 - (-1.5)) = 0.5 / 2 = 0.25. v1 is three times as far behind the plane as v0 is in front, so the cut is a quarter of the way along.

wrong.feedback: That is measured from v1. From v0, t = 0.5 / 2 = 0.25.
The cut isn't halfway: v0 is 0.5 in front and v1 1.5 behind, so the cut is a quarter of the way from v0.

8e2.question: A fresh case. Corners have z + w of -0.4, 1.6 and 1.6. On the edge v0 -> v1, at what fraction t of the way from v0 is the cut?

wrong.feedback: That is measured from v1. From v0, t = 0.4 / 2 = 0.2.

8f.question: A cache set with 2 ways, empty at first, gets accesses to lines A, B, A, C, A. How many misses does least recently used replacement count?
8f.reason: A misses, B misses, A hits and becomes the most recently used, so C evicts B, the least recently used, and the last A hits. 3 misses and 2 hits.

wrong.feedback: That evicts A at C, the line that arrived first. Least recently used looks at the last access: A was used after B, so B leaves and the last A hits. 3.
The second A finds A still in the set: a hit. So does the last one. 3 misses.
C is new, so it misses too and must evict a line: A, B and C miss. 3.

8f2.question: A fresh case. The same set gets A, B, C, B, A, C. How many misses?
8f2.reason: A, B miss. C misses and evicts A. B hits. A misses and evicts C, now the least recently used. C misses and evicts B. 5 misses, 1 hit.

wrong.feedback: That evicts by arrival order. After B's hit, C is the least recently used, so A evicts C and the last C misses: 5.
A comes back after C evicted it, and C after A evicted it: 5 misses.

9a.section: Five halls you have not seen
9a.question: Two triangles cover a pixel at exactly the same depth. Which one's id must the pixel hold? (a) the one drawn first, (b) the one drawn second, (c) whichever covers more of the tile, (d) either, the check accepts both.
9a.reason: The depth test is LESS: a fragment wins only if it is strictly nearer than what is stored. At equal depth the second draw loses, so the first drawn keeps the pixel, as lesson 3's equal-depth rule says and both measured GPUs do.

wrong.feedback: That is LEQUAL. Under LESS an equal depth fails the test, so the first drawn keeps the pixel.
The depth test decides pixel by pixel, and an equal depth goes to the first drawn.
The ids must match exactly, so the rule has to be fixed: LESS, the first drawn wins.

9a2.question: A fresh case. A triangle drawn later is strictly nearer at a pixel than the one drawn first. Which id does the pixel hold? (a) the first, (b) the later one.
9a2.reason: Strictly nearer passes LESS, whatever the order: the later, nearer triangle owns the pixel.

wrong.feedback: Draw order decides only exact ties. A strictly nearer fragment passes the depth test.

9b.question: In the final picture, the eight pixels of one block show triangles 3, 3, 7, 7, 7, the background, 3 and 9. How many visible warps does that block add?
9b.reason: Count the different triangles that own at least one pixel of the block: 3, 7 and 9. The background isn't a triangle. 3 visible warps.

wrong.feedback: That counts pixels with a triangle. Visible warps count different triangles: 3, 7 and 9.
The background is no triangle and needs no shading: 3, 7 and 9 make 3.
One warp shades all the lanes of one triangle in the block, so triangles 3, 7 and 9 need 3 warps.

9b2.question: A fresh case. A block's pixels show triangles 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4. How many visible warps?
9b2.reason: Four different triangles own pixels of the block: 4.

wrong.feedback: Count triangles, not pixels: 1, 2, 3 and 4.
Four different triangles appear: 4.

9c.question: On practice hall 1, a renderer shades every fragment that passes the depth test, in draw order. About how many times the shading budget of 4,021 warps does it launch? (a) under the budget, (b) about 1.5 times, (c) about 3 to 5 times, (d) about 20 times.
9c.reason: It launches 14,029 warps, 3.49 times the budget: most pixels near the camera are shaded once for every screen behind them that passed the depth test when it arrived, and only the last shading survives.

wrong.feedback: Testing depth before shading doesn't stop a nearer triangle drawn later from being shaded over farther ones already shaded: 14,029 warps.
Most pixels have several screens behind them, each shaded in turn as it arrived: 3.49 times the budget.
Depth testing still rejects fragments behind what is already drawn, which keeps it to 3.49 times.

9c2.question: A fresh case. Practice hall 2 has 3,128 visible warps, a budget of 3,910. Shaded in draw order it launches 14,208 warps. About how many times the budget? (a) under, (b) about 1.5, (c) about 3 to 5, (d) about 20.

4a.question: A texture is 4 texels wide. Which texel column does nearest sampling pick at u = 0.6?
4a.reason: u × w = 2.4, and nearest takes floor(2.4) = 2: texel 2 covers u from 0.5 to 0.75.

wrong.feedback: That rounds 2.4 up, as Math.ceil does. Texel 2 covers u from 0.5 to 0.75, so floor(u × w) = 2 is the texel that holds the point.
u × w = 2.4, so the point is in texel 2, which covers 2 to 3 in texel units.

4a2.question: A fresh case. 8 texels wide, u = 0.99. Which column?

wrong.feedback: Texel 8 would be past the edge: floor(7.92) = 7.

4b.question: A texture is 4 texels wide. Which texel column does nearest sampling pick at u = -0.3?
4b.reason: u × w = -1.2, floor gives -2, and repeating wraps -2 to 4 - 2 = 2.

wrong.feedback: That clamps to the edge. The course's textures repeat: texel -2 is texel 2.
floor(-1.2) is -2, not -1: floor rounds down, towards minus infinity. -2 wraps to 2.
Texel -2 doesn't exist: repeating wraps it to 4 - 2 = 2.

4b2.question: A fresh case. 4 texels wide, u = 1.25. Which column?

wrong.feedback: Clamping would give the last texel. Repeating wraps 5 to 1.

4c.question: A texture is 4 texels wide. At u = 0.4, what weight does bilinear filtering give texel column 2?
4c.reason: x = u × w - 0.5 = 1.1, so x0 = 1 and fx = 0.1. Texel 1 gets 1 - fx = 0.9 and texel 2 gets fx = 0.1: the point is close to texel 1's centre.

wrong.feedback: That is texel 1's weight. Texel 2 is the far one: fx = 0.1.
That leaves out the half-texel step. x = u × w - 0.5 = 1.1, so fx = 0.1.
Weights come from x = u × w - 0.5 = 1.1, not from u itself: texel 2 gets 0.1.

4c2.question: A fresh case. 4 texels wide, u = 0.5. What weight does texel column 1 get?
4c2.reason: x = 2 - 0.5 = 1.5, so texels 1 and 2 each get 0.5: u = 0.5 is exactly between their centres.

wrong.feedback: u = 0.5 is the edge between texels 1 and 2, halfway between their centres: 0.5 each.
x = 1.5: texel 1 is one of the two blended, with weight 0.5.

4d.question: A floor triangle's edge runs from a corner with w = 1 and u = 0 to a corner with w = 4 and u = 1. Nearest sampling a texture 16 texels wide, which texel column does the pixel halfway between them on screen pick?
4d.reason: Perspective-correct, q = 0.5 and 0.5 / 4 = 0.125, so u = 0.125 / 0.625 = 0.2. Then floor(0.2 × 16) = floor(3.2) = 3.

wrong.feedback: That uses the screen-weight u, 0.5. The perspective-correct u is 0.2: texel 3.
That weights the near corner less. The far corner, w = 4, gets the smaller weight: u = 0.2, texel 3.
u × 16 = 3.2, and nearest takes floor: 3.

4d2.question: A fresh case. An edge runs from a corner with w = 2 and u = 0 to a corner with w = 6 and u = 1. For the pixel halfway between them on screen, which column does nearest sampling pick in a texture 16 texels wide?

wrong.feedback: Screen weights give 0.5. Perspective-correct, u = 0.25: texel 4.

4e.question: Two pictures of four pixels. In pixel 0 both drew triangle 5, and green differs by 2 levels. In pixel 1 yours drew triangle 5, theirs triangle 6, and the colours are 190 levels apart. In pixel 2 both left background. In pixel 3 both drew triangle 6, 1 level apart. What maxLevel does diffImages return?
4e.reason: Pixel 1 is a coverage mismatch, so its colour isn't compared: two different triangles are expected to differ in colour. Background isn't compared either. Of pixels 0 and 3, the largest difference is 2 levels.

wrong.feedback: Pixel 1 belongs to different triangles, a coverage mismatch: its colour isn't compared. maxLevel looks only where both drew the same triangle: 2.
Pixel 0 differs by 2 levels in green, and maxLevel keeps the largest: 2.
Pixels 0 and 3 are compared: the largest difference is 2.

4e2.question: A fresh case. Pixel 0: same triangle, 0 levels apart. Pixel 1: different triangles, 50 levels apart. Pixel 2: same triangle, 3 levels apart. What overOne does diffImages return?
4e2.reason: Only pixels drawn by the same triangle are compared: pixel 2 is more than 1 level off, pixel 0 isn't. Pixel 1 counts in coverage instead.

wrong.feedback: Pixel 1 is a coverage mismatch, so its colour isn't compared: only pixel 2 counts.
Pixel 2 differs by 3 levels, more than 1.

4f.question: Suppose the reference courtyard is drawn at 1/16 instead of 1/256 and compared with the Apple GPU. About how many pixels differ in triangle ownership? (a) 0, (b) 1, (c) about 50, (d) about 5,000.
4f.reason: The courtyard's corners land anywhere after the divide, so most of them snap to a slightly different place on the two grids, and the pixels whose centres lie within a step of an edge can change owner. On the recorded run, 51 pixels differ, all beside an edge.

wrong.feedback: Both grids are allowed by WebGL, but they put most corners in slightly different places, and pixels beside the edges follow them: 51 on the recorded run.
One pixel is what's left when your pipeline runs on the GPU's own grid. On the wrong grid, 51 differ.
A corner moves by less than 1/16 of a pixel, so only pixels within a step of an edge can change: 51, not thousands.

4f2.question: A fresh case. Suppose the reference is drawn at 1/256 instead and compared with SwiftShader, which snaps to 1/16. About how many pixels differ? (a) 0, (b) 1, (c) about 50, (d) about 5,000.
4f2.reason: The same two grids as in 4f, swapped. Drawn in Node at stage 4, the reference courtyard at 1/16 and at 1/256 gives 52 pixels to different triangles; lesson 4's recorded run, the reference at 1/16 against the Apple GPU at 1/256, found 51.

wrong.feedback: The grids differ, so the corners land in different places: about 50 pixels differ.

4t.question: Suppose the phone reports the top-left rule and a grid of 1/64. Drawn at 1/16, which of unit 4's scenes would your pictures need to change to match it exactly, bands aside? (a) none, (b) the courtyard only, (c) the tie scenes only, (d) all of them.
4t.reason: The tie scenes and the coplanar pair have their corners on the 1/16 grid, and every 1/16 point is also a 1/64 point, so they snap to the same places and the tie rule is the same. The courtyard's corners land anywhere after the divide, so they move.

wrong.feedback: The courtyard's corners, which land anywhere after the divide, snap to other places on a 1/64 grid.
The tie scenes' corners sit on the 1/16 grid, which a 1/64 grid contains, and the tie rule is the same, so they don't change.
A corner already on the 1/16 grid stays put on the finer 1/64 grid. Only the courtyard moves.

4t2.question: A fresh case. A GPU on the 1/16 grid uses the mirrored tie rule: it nudges a centre left and down instead of right and up. How many pixels of the shared-diagonal scene change owner?
4t2.reason: Every pixel whose centre lies exactly on an edge goes to the other triangle, or to none: the shared-diagonal scene has 237 such tie pixels, and all of them change.

wrong.feedback: That counts only the diagonal. The square's outer edges pass through pixel centres too: 237 tie pixels in all.
